analysis.one_liner: Bars insurance companies and pharmacy benefit managers from owning pharmacies, to separate drug pricing middlemen from the pharmacies they steer patients toward.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in December 2024 with one Republican cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for one company to own both a pharmacy and a health insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and decide which pharmacies are in insurance networks. Big companies that own insurers, PBMs, and pharmacies under one roof would have three years to sell off the pharmacies. Regulators and state attorneys general could sue to enforce the split and claw back pharmacy revenue earned during a violation, with that money redirected to help the overcharged community. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent and community pharmacies, which compete against PBM-owned mail-order and chain pharmacies that can be favored within insurance networks; and patients, who could see lower drug prices and better access if PBM-owned pharmacies can no longer be steered business by the same company negotiating prices.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for one company to own both a pharmacy and an insurance company or PBM, with violators required to divest the pharmacy within three years.

It lets the FTC, the Justice Department's antitrust division, HHS's Inspector General, and state attorneys general sue violators and force them to disgorge drug revenue collected during the violation, with that money redirected to serve the health needs of the overcharged community.
It requires FTC and Justice Department review of any divestiture to ensure the buyer does not recreate the same concentration, and directs the FTC to write rules enforcing the prohibition.

analysis.who_pays: Large insurers and PBMs that own pharmacy chains would have to divest those pharmacies within three years, absorbing the disruption and lost integration revenue of the split.

drawbacks.text: Forcing integrated companies to sell their pharmacies within three years could disrupt services at stores currently owned by insurers and PBMs—including mail-order and specialty pharmacies—while divestitures are arranged, and integration savings that those companies claim to pass along would be lost.

Prohibiting the ownership structure directly, rather than the specific practices (like reimbursement differences or steering), is a blunt tool; defenders of integrated models argue the conduct itself can be addressed through existing antitrust and pharmacy-reform laws without mandating divestiture.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a structural fix to a documented conflict of interest: PBMs that also own pharmacies have an incentive to steer patients to their own stores and pay themselves better than rivals, which raises costs for patients and helps close independent pharmacies. The main cost is disruption—forced divestitures within three years, with divested chains changing hands and integration savings (however much they actually reach consumers) lost; some argue antitrust or PBM-reform laws already address the conduct. The bill targets the structural problem rather than every pricing practice, so it would not by itself fix all PBM pricing, but it is a narrow, enforceable prohibition with defined oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2024 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no vote or hearing before Congress ended weeks later.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on December 12, 2024, with less than a month left in the 118th Congress.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It drew one cosponsor, Senator Josh Hawley (R), in addition to sponsor Senator Elizabeth Warren (D).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the large insurers that own integrated pharmacy chains; nothing changed for them, and they keep the ability to steer drug sales to their own pharmacies.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit common ownership of PBMs, insurers, and pharmacies.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or floor vote for the three weeks remaining in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: With only two sponsors — one Democrat and one Republican — and no committee action or votes, no party-line pattern ever emerged.

industries.note: The bill forbids PBMs from owning pharmacies and requires divestiture of existing pharmacy holdings within three years, ending their control of both the pricing middleman role and the dispensing side. Consumers could benefit if the conflict of interest between negotiating drug prices and filling prescriptions is removed.

industries.industry: Integrated insurers (e.g., companies that own insurers, PBMs, and pharmacy chains)
industries.note: Health insurers that also own pharmacies and PBMs would have to sell the pharmacy businesses, reducing their vertical integration. Ordinary patients could gain from more honest price negotiation, but the transition would disrupt how they currently receive drugs.

Independent pharmacies compete against PBM-owned chains that can favor their own stores in network placement and reimbursement. Removing that conflict of interest levels the competitive field for them.
